readings.c3s1:
¶
'''traveling-cabinet''' (trav′el-ing-kab″i-net), ''n.'' A small chest of drawers, of which the drawers and other compartments are secured by outer doors, and which could be carried easily by a man on horseback or in other ways. Cabinets of this kind were common in the seventeenth century, and were often richly decorated.

'''traveling-cap''' (trav′el-ing-kap), ''n.'' A soft cap of a form convenient for travelers.

'''traveling-carriage''' (trav′el-ing-kar″ạ̄j), ''n.'' A large and heavy four-wheeled carriage, fitted with imperials and a rumble, and used for journeys before the introduction of railways.

{{smaller block|Lucy and Mr. Talboys cantered gaily along; Mr. Fountain rolled after in a phaeton; the ''travelling-carriage'' came last.
{{right|''C. Reade'', Love me Little, x.}}}}

'''traveling-chest''' (trav′el-ing-chest), ''n.'' A coffer or large box, often richly decorated, made for containing personal property on a journey.

'''traveling-couvert''' (trav′el-ing-kö-vãr′), ''n.'' A set of table utensils, as knife, fork, spoon, and drinking-cup, made to pack closely, for use in traveling. {{smaller|The longer articles were sometimes made so as to separate into two parts, or with hinges by which they could be closed together for convenience in packing.}}

'''traveling-dress''' (trav′el-ing-dres), ''n.'' A dress of plain and serviceable material and commodious fit, to be worn in traveling.

{{smaller block|The darker mélanges are made into ''travelling'' and beach ''dresses'' and long wraps for summer jaunts.
{{right|''New York Evening Post'', April 25, 1891.}}}}

'''travelled, traveller''', etc. See ''traveled'', etc.

'''travelous†''' (trav′el-us), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''travailous''; < ME. ''travelous'', ''travallous'', ''travalous'', < OF. *''travaillous'', < ''travail'', labor: see

{{RunningHeader|travel|6445|traverse}}{{smaller block|How difficult it was to ''travel'' where no license made it safe, where no preparations in roads, inns, carriages, made it convenient.{{right|''De Quincey'', Style, ii.}}}} ¶ 3. Specifically, to make a journey or go about from place to place for the purpose of taking orders for goods, collecting accounts, etc., for a commercial house. {{smaller block|Brown Brothers, of Snow Hill, were substantial people, and Mr. Snengkeld ''travelled'' in strict accordance with the good old rules of trade.{{right|''Trollope'', Orley Farm, ix.}}}} 4. In ''mech.'', to traverse; move over a fixed distance, as a movable part of a machine. See ''travel'', ''n.'', 5.—5. To proceed or advance in any way; pass from one point to another; move; wander: as, his eye ''traveled'' over the landscape; also, to move at a specified gait, pace, or rate: as, that horse ''travels'' wide. {{smaller block|Time ''travels'' in divers paces with divers persons.{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 2. 326.}}}} {{smaller block|News ''travelled'' with increase from mouth to mouth.{{right|''Pope'', Temple of Fame, l. 474.}}}} {{smaller block|The home manufacture of gas . . . is a part of the inventor's scheme which does not entirely depend for success upon the power of gas to ''travel''.{{right|''Ure'', Dict., II. 538.}}}} 6. To walk. [Colloq.]—7. To move onward in feeding; browse from one point to another: said of deer, etc. {{smaller block|If the deer is ''travelling'', as it is called, one has to walk much faster, and scan the ground as best he can.{{right|''Sportsman's Gazetteer'', p. 88.}}}} '''To sue, labor, and travel.''' {{smaller|See ''sue''1.}}—'''To travel bodkin.''' {{smaller|See ''bodkin''1.}}—'''To travel dak.''' {{smaller|See ''dak''.}}—'''To travel out of the record,''' {{smaller|to stray from the point, or from the prescribed or authorized line of discussion.}} {{smaller block|I have ''travelled out of the record'', sir, I am aware, in putting the point to you.{{right|''Dickens'', Little Dorrit, ii. 28.}}}} {{smaller|'''Traveling-apron oven.''' See ''oven''.}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To harass; trouble; plague; torment. {{smaller block|If a man be ''traueylid'' with a feend, and may not be delyuerid fro him, lete him drinke a litil quantite of oure 5 essence. {{right|''Book of Quinte Essence'' (ed. Furnivall), p. 19.}}}} {{smaller block|Such a distemper as ''travailed'' me at Paris: a fever, and dysentery. {{right|''Donne'', Letters, xxxvii.}}}} {{smaller block|As if all these troubles had not been sufficient to ''travail'' the realm, a great division fell among the nobility. {{right|''Hayward.'' (''Johnson.'')}}}} '''2.''' To journey through; pass over; make the tour of: as, to ''travel'' the whole kingdom of England. {{smaller block|These, and a thousand more such sleights, have hypocrisie learned by ''trauailing'' strange countries. {{right|''Nashe'', Pierce Penilesse, p. 68.}}}} {{smaller block|He had subsequently ''travelled'' New England and the Middle States, as a pedler, in the employment of a Connecticut manufactory of cologne-water and other essences. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xii.}}}} '''3.''' To cause or force to journey, or move from place to place. {{smaller block|They [the corporations] shall not be ''travelled'' forth of their own franchises. {{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}} {{smaller block|Their horses are but smal, but very swift & hard; they ''trauell'' them vnshod both winter and Sommer. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', I. 479.}}}} {{smaller block|Landholders, most of whom are owners of sheep which have to be ''travelled'' twice a year. {{right|''W. Shepherd'', Prairie Experiences, p. 152.}}}} '''traveled, travelled''' (trav′eld), ''p. a.'' [Pp. of ''travel'', ''v.''] '''1†.''' Harassed; tormented; fretted. {{smaller block|It is here to be understoode, euerie yoke naturally to bee heauie, sharpe, harde, and painefull: and the beast that draweth the same goeth bound and ''trauelled''. {{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 47.}}}} '''2.''' Worked over; turned up with the spade; tilled. {{smaller block|"It's ''travelled'' earth, that," said Edie; "it howks sae eithly. I ken it weel, for ance I wrought a simmer wi' auld Will Winnett, the bedral, and howkit mair graves than ane in my day." {{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, xxiii.}}}} '''3.''' Having made journeys; having gone, or having been carried, to distant points or countries: as, ''traveled'' Madeira is highly prized. {{smaller block|From Latian syrens, French Circæan feasts, Return well ''travell'd'', and transform'd to beasts. {{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Horace, I. vi. 123.}}}} {{smaller block|One whose Arab face was tanned By tropic sun and boreal frost, So ''travelled'' there was scarce a land Or people left him to exhaust. {{right|''Whittier'', Tent on the Beach.}}}} '''4.''' Having gained knowledge or experience by labor or travel; hence, experienced; knowing. {{smaller block|I am not much ''travelled'' in the history of modern times. {{right|''Fielding''. (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}} {{smaller block|A man of fashion, too, he made his tour, Learn'd vive la bagatelle, et vive l'amour; So ''travell'd'' monkeys their grimace improve. {{right|''Burns'', A Sketch.}}}} '''traveler, traveller''' (trav′el-ėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''travaillour'', < OF. ''travailleur'', F. ''travailleur'', a laborer, toiler, < ''travailler'', labor: see ''travel''.] '''1'''†. A toiler; laborer; worker. {{smaller block|It is therefore no smal benefite that suche persones dooe to a common weale, which are willingly ''trauailers'' in this kinde of writing. {{right|''Udall'', Pref. to K. Edw. VI.}}}} 2. One who or that which travels in any way; one who makes a journey, or who is on his way from place to place; a wayfarer; one who or that which gets over the ground: as, his horse is a good ''traveler''. {{smaller block|O ''traveller'', stay thy weary feet,
Drink of this fountain pure and sweet. {{right|''Longfellow'', Inscription on Drinking Fountain at Shanklin, Isle of Wight.}}}} 3. One who journeys to foreign lands; one who visits strange countries and people. {{smaller block|When a ''traveller'' returneth home, let him not leave the countries where he hath travelled altogether behind him, but maintain a correspondence by letters. {{right|''Bacon'', Travel (ed. 1887).}} Sometimes we had rather believe a ''traveller's'' lie than go to disprove him. {{right|''Donne'', Letters, xvii.}}}} 4. A person who travels for a mercantile firm to solicit orders for goods, collect accounts, and the like. Also called ''commercial traveler'', and formerly ''rider''. {{smaller block|John Kenneby . . . had at last got into the house of Hubbles and Grease, and had risen to be their bookkeeper. He had once been tried by them as a ''traveller'', but in that line he had failed. {{right|''Trollope'', Orley Farm, xxiv.}}}} 5. Same as ''swagman'', 2. [Australia.]—6. That which travels or traverses. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') ''Naut.'': (1) An iron ring or thimble fitted to traverse freely on a rope, spar, or metal rod, and used for various purposes on shipboard. (2) A rod fastened to the deck on which a thimble carrying the sheet of a fore-and-aft sail may slide from side to side of the vessel, or a rod or rope up and down a mast along which a yard may slide. (''b'') A crab on a long beam moving on wheels on an elevated}} track in a stone-yard, workshop, etc. {{smaller|It is often used with a differential pulley for raising and moving heavy weights, and is a device of the nature of the traveling crane. See third cut under ''pulley.'' (''c'') In ''ring-spinning'', a small metal ring or loop used to guide the yarn in winding it upon the spindle. (''d'') ''Theat.'', moving mechanism above the stage for carrying fairies and apparitions.—'''Commercial traveler.''' See def. 4.—'''Ring-and-traveler spinner.''' Same as ''ring-frame.''—'''To tip the traveler,''' to humbug: in allusion to travelers' tales or yarns. [Slang.]}} {{smaller block|"I'd rather see you dead than brought to such a dilemma." "Mayhap thou wouldst," answered the uncle; "for then, my lad, there would be some picking; aha! dost thou ''tip'' me ''the traveller'', my boy?" {{right|''Smollett'', Sir L. Greaves, vi. (''Davies.'')}}}} {{smaller|'''Traveler's hut,''' the quarters provided on every Australian station for persons traveling on the road who are not of a class to be asked to the squatter's house, such as stockmen and swagmen. [Australia.]}} '''traveler's-joy''' (trav′el-ėrz-joi), ''n.'' The virgin's-bower, ''Clematis Vitalba'': so named as climbing over hedges and adorning the way. {{smaller|This is a vigorous species, with a woody stem sometimes as thick as the wrist, and widely climbing branches. Its inner bark is used in Switzerland for straining milk; the slender shoots in France serve to bind fagots; while the young tips are sometimes pickled. An infusion of the roots and stems in boiling oil is a successful application for itch. Also called ''lady's-bower.'' See cut under ''virgin's-bower.''}} {{smaller block|One [cottage], . . . summer-blanch'd, Was parcel-bearded with the ''traveler's-joy'' In Autumn, parcel ivy-clad. {{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer's Field.}}}} '''traveler's-tree''' (trav′el-ėrz-trē), ''n.'' A tree of Madagascar, ''Ravenala Madagascariensis'': thus named as furnishing drink from its hollow leaf-stalks. See ''Ravenala.'' '''traveling, travelling''' (trav′el-ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''travel'', ''v.''] 1†. The act of laboring; labor; toil. {{smaller block|He . . . wolde ich reneyede begging
And lyvede by my ''traveylyng.''{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6788.}}}} 2. The act of making a journey, especially in foreign countries. {{smaller block|In ''travelling'' by land there is a continuity of scene, and a connected succession of persons and incidents, that carry on the story of life, and lessen the effect of absence and separation.{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 17.}}}} 3. Motion of any kind; change of place; passage. {{smaller block|The mains in the streets are nearly five miles in length, and the gas is said to bear ''travelling'' through this length of pipe very well.{{right|''Ure'', Dict., II. 538.}}}} '''traveling, travelling''' (trav′el-ing), ''p. a.'' 1. Itinerant; peddling. {{smaller block|By and by there 's the ''travelling'' doctor gives pills, lets blood, draws teeth.{{right|''Browning'', Up at a Villa.}}}} 2. Movable; moving: as, a ''traveling'' crane. See ''crane''2, 1.—3. ''Naut.'', movable from place to place on a traveler.—'''Traveling backstays.''' {{smaller|See ''backstay''.}}—'''Traveling elder.''' {{smaller|See ''elder''1, 5 (''c'').}}—'''Traveling forge, gauntree, post-office,''' etc. {{smaller|See the nouns.}} '''traveling-bag''' (trav′el-ing-bag), ''n.'' A bag or wallet, usually of leather, for carrying necessaries on a journey: sometimes provided with a special set of toilet articles, and then known in the trade as a ''fitted'' bag. '''traveling-cabinet''' (trav′el-ing-kab″i-net), ''n.'' A small chest of drawers, of which the drawers and other compartments are secured by outer doors, and which could be carried easily by a man on horseback or in other ways. Cabinets of this kind were common in the seventeenth century, and were often richly decorated. '''traveling-cap''' (trav′el-ing-kap), ''n.'' A soft cap of a form convenient for travelers. '''traveling-carriage''' (trav′el-ing-kar″ạ̄j), ''n.'' A large and heavy four-wheeled carriage, fitted with imperials and a rumble, and used for journeys before the introduction of railways. {{smaller block|Lucy and Mr. Talboys cantered gaily along; Mr. Fountain rolled after in a phaeton; the ''travelling-carriage'' came last. {{right|''C. Reade'', Love me Little, x.}}}} '''traveling-chest''' (trav′el-ing-chest), ''n.'' A coffer or large box, often richly decorated, made for containing personal property on a journey. '''traveling-couvert''' (trav′el-ing-kö-vãr′), ''n.'' A set of table utensils, as knife, fork, spoon, and drinking-cup, made to pack closely, for use in traveling. {{smaller|The longer articles were sometimes made so as to separate into two parts, or with hinges by which they could be closed together for convenience in packing.}} '''traveling-dress''' (trav′el-ing-dres), ''n.'' A dress of plain and serviceable material and commodious fit, to be worn in traveling. {{smaller block|The darker mélanges are made into ''travelling'' and beach ''dresses'' and long wraps for summer jaunts. {{right|''New York Evening Post'', April 25, 1891.}}}} '''travelled, traveller''', etc. See ''traveled'', etc. '''travelous†''' (trav′el-us), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''travailous''; < ME. ''travelous'', ''travallous'', ''travalous'', < OF. *''travaillous'', < ''travail'', labor: see ''travel'', ''n.''] Laborious; toilsome. {{smaller block|We are accustomed in the begynnynge of dyggynge of mynes especially to caule for the grace of god that it may please hym to be presente with his ayde to owre doubtfull and ''traualious'' [read ''trauailous''] woorke. {{right|''R. Eden'', tr. of Vannuccio Biringuccio (First Books on [America, ed. Arber, p. 357).}}}} '''travel-soiled''' (trav′el-soild), ''a.'' Same as ''travel-stained.'' {{smaller block|All dripping from the recent flood,
Panting and ''travel-soil'd'' he stood. {{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iii. 21.}}}} '''travel-stained''' (trav′el-stānd), ''a.'' Having the clothes, etc., stained with the marks of travel. '''travel-tainted†''' (trav′el-tān″ted), ''a.'' Same as ''travel-stained.'' {{smaller block|I have foundered nine score and odd posts; and here, ''travel-tainted'' as I am, have, in my pure and immaculate valour, taken Sir John Coleville. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 3. 40.}}}} '''travel-worn''' (trav′el-wōrn), ''a.'' Fatigued and disheveled by traveling. {{smaller block|From all that elegant crowd of travellers he . . . picked us out, the only two in the least disreputable and ''travel-worn.'' {{right|''Harper's Mag.'', LXXVII. 494.}}}} '''traverst†''', ''a.'', ''n.'', and ''adv.'' An obsolete variant of ''traverse.'' '''traversable''' (trav′ėr-sa-bl), ''a.'' [< ''traverse'' + ''-able.''] 1. Capable of being traversed or crossed. {{smaller block|Most of Toledo is ''traversable'' only for pedestrians and donkeys. {{right|''Lathrop'', Spanish Vistas, p. 36.}}}} 2. Capable of being traversed or denied: as, a ''traversable'' allegation. {{smaller block|As to presentments of petty offences in the town or leet, Lord Mansfield has said that it cannot be true that they are not ''traversable'' anywhere. {{right|''Sir J. T. Coleridge'', Note on Blackstone's Com., IV. xxiii.}}}} '''3.''' In ''law'' (of an allegation in pleading), such that traversing or denying entitles to trial as an issue of fact, as distinguished from an allegation which is not material, or which relates only to the measure of damages. '''traversant†''' (trav′ėr-sạnt), ''a.'' [ME. ''traversaunt'', < OF. ''traversant'', ppr. of ''traverser'', traverse: see ''traverse'', ''v.'', and cf. ''transversant''.] Cross; thwart; unfavorable. {{smaller block|Thou hast a dominacioun ''traversaunt'', Wythowte numbre doyst thou greeve. {{right|''MS. Cantab.'' Ff. i. 6, f. 137. (''Halliwell.'')}}}} '''traverse''' (trav′ėrs), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''travers'', < OF. ''travers'', F. ''travers'', lying across, thwart, transverse (''travers'', m., a breadth, in mod. F. irregularity, etc., ''traverse'', f., a cross-bar, cross-road, etc.), = Pr. ''travers'', ''transvers'' = Sp. ''travesío'' = Pg. ''travesso'' = It. ''traverso'', < L. ''traversus'', ''transversus'', lying across, transverse: see ''transverse'', of which ''traverse'' is a doublet.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Situated or acting across or athwart; thwart; transverse; crossing. {{smaller block|Trees . . . hewen downe, and layde ''trauers'', one ouer auother. ''Berners'', tr. of Froissart's Chron., II. clxxxvi.}} {{smaller block|The paths cut with ''traverse'' trenches much encumbered the carriages. {{right|''Sir J. Hayward.''}}}}
